Chapter Four: The Internalization of Authority and the Loss of Self.
As you move through life, have you ever noticed how the voices of authority—like parents, teachers, bosses, or even so-called experts—somehow start echoing inside your own head? Over time, those outside voices blend right into your thoughts, quietly shaping what you believe, what you want, and even how you see yourself.
It happens so slowly, so quietly, that most of us don’t even realize it’s going on. Let’s picture a student for a moment—maybe someone you know, or maybe even you at a younger age. She starts out bright-eyed and curious, full of questions and excitement about the world. But as she gets older, she learns to hold back, to ask only the “right” questions, and to steer clear of anything that might make adults uneasy. Suddenly, the boundaries of what’s okay to ask or think become crystal clear, and she adapts—shaping her interests just to fit in with what others expect.
But here’s something to pay attention to: internalizing authority isn’t only about following rules. It’s really about taking on the values, beliefs, and priorities of other people as if they were your own. Most of us walk around thinking we’re making our own choices, but if you look a little closer, you’ll see that many of our decisions just echo the preferences of those in charge.
There’s a story that really brings this to life. Imagine a man who spends his whole life chasing what everyone calls “success.” He works nonstop, climbs the corporate ladder, and collects all the shiny symbols—a big house, a luxury car, a fancy title. But deep down, he feels empty. Why? Because the goals he’s been chasing were never really his. They were handed down from parents, teachers, and society. He followed the script, but it never brought the satisfaction he thought it would.
That’s the real danger here—the loss of self. People end up feeling like strangers in their own lives, living out routines that don’t actually reflect who they are or what they truly want. They push down their own dreams and needs, convinced that fitting in is the price they have to pay for acceptance.
And it doesn’t stop there. Social pressure keeps the cycle going. When someone tries to break free, they might face criticism, ridicule, or even be left out. The fear of standing out is powerful enough to keep most folks in line, even when it means giving up on their own happiness.
But think about this: when people hide their true selves, it’s not just individuals who lose out—society does too. Progress, creativity, and real innovation need lots of different voices and new ideas. When everyone thinks and acts the same, the world just gets stuck.
So, how do you reclaim that sense of self? It takes courage. You have to be willing to question old beliefs, try new things, and step outside your comfort zone. It means listening to your own voice, even if it goes against what you’ve always been told. And it’s about valuing authenticity over approval, and growth over staying safe.
A lot of people never take that leap—they’re content to live within the lines drawn by others. But for those who do, the rewards are real. They find a sense of purpose, and a kind of fulfillment, that you just can’t get from simply fitting in. True freedom isn’t about breaking every rule—it’s about living in alignment with what really matters to you.
